To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensitivity of arthropod species to pyrethoids is determined by the combination of body size and preference for coarse substrata, that the sensitivity of nonarthropods is low, and that the existing ecotoxicity database is inadequate to predict the sensitivity of untested species.
the pyrethroids λ-cyhallothrin and bifenthrin are highly toxic to most arthropod species (LC50 0.01-1.0 μg L(-l)), whereas nonarthopod species were insensitive (LC50 >10 μg L-1).
the sensitivity of freshwater invertebrates to pyrethoids is determined by species characteristics such as body size and substrate preferences.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of how the use of nonstandard test species for pesticide toxicity testing could improve the ecological relevance and predictive power of ecotoxicological data, and we provide evidence for the importance of species characteristics in determining the sensitivity to pyrethoids.
the development of trait-based approaches for predicting ecotoxicological effects of pyrethroids in nonstandard test species.
the development of trait-based ecotoxicology and its potential to provide a mechanistic understanding of the sensitivity of species to toxic chemicals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
trait characteristics determine pyrethroid toxicity in freshwater macroinvertebrates.
pyrethroids are highly toxic to aquatic invertebrates, but the sensitivity of species is highly variable and depends on species-specific traits.
pyrethroid toxicity varies greatly among species, and that the most important factors determining pyrethroid susceptibility are body size and habitat preference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
trait characteristics determine pyrethroid sensitivities in nonstandard test species of freshwater macroinvertebrates.
pyrethroid toxicity to macroinvertebrates can be predicted with a high level of confidence for some taxa, but not for others.
the pyrethroids are not a homogenous group of chemicals, and that the ecotoxicity of pyrethroids cannot be extrapolated to all aquatic species.
The main takeaway from our work is that

pyrethroid sensitivities vary considerably among freshwater invertebrates and that trait characteristics are important determinants of pyrethroid toxicity in species that have not previously been tested.

pyrethroid sensitivities are species-specific, and that pyrethroids may have a much greater effect on macroinvertebrate communities than previously anticipated, especially in coarse-gravel substrates.
trait characteristics, and not taxonomic relatedness, determine pyrethroid toxicity in nonstandard test species.
